newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's union group delays public-sector strike.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's union group delays public-sector strike.

text.p: South Korea's outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions (KFTU) said on Sunday it would delay strikes by some public-sector union workers to minimise inconvenience to the public.
The confederation had said earlier that unions at state-run corporations, the subway, hospitals and broadcasting companies would join in strikes from Tuesday.

However KFTU spokesman Kim Yoo-sun said: "We decided to postpone strikes at subways, the state-run Korea Telecom and the Korea Mint Corp. Our enemy is the Kim Young-sam government and not (the) people."

Thousands of unionised workers staged rallies in big cities including Seoul and Pusan to back their demand for the repeal of a controversial labour law which gives employers the right to lay off employees, hire temporary workers and replace strikers.
Witnesses said the number of protesters had dropped sharply from Saturday when about 5,000 gathered in Seoul alone.

About 200 unions at the nation's major car makers, ship builders and secondary financial institutions, representing 230,000 members, will go on strike from Monday morning as scheduled, the confederation said.
"From Tuesday, workers at hospitals and broadcasting companies will join in the work stoppage," said Kim.
The confederation and the nation's largest union group Federation of Korea Trade Unions (FKTU) said they would escalate industrial action until the government repeals the law.
The government argues that changes in the law would benefit unions and employers by creating a more flexible labour market.
The two umbrella union groups between them claim a total membership of 1.7 million in most of South Korea's major industries and public-sector services.
Nationwide strikes erupted on December 26 after the ruling New Korea Party pushed through the new labour law during a clandestine session of parliament.
The stoppages, which hit car and ship production, hospitals and subways, were suspended until after the New Year holidays in a goodwill gesture to the public.
The more moderate Federation of Korean Trade Unions has also announced it plans a large-scale rally on January 10 and a general strike by all of its members a day later.
The body said its second round of strikes would be led by unions in the public and service sectors.
